title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: the gods and the demons were at war, and the gods reached for a song. the Chandogya tells which breath could carry it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the Chandogya's chain: earth, water, plants, people, speech, verse, melody, and at the end the high chant, Om. Which chain did you follow back? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

The gods and the demons were at war. That's how the story starts, in the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad, the text of the Sama Veda we opened yesterday. Both sides are children of the same creator. Both want to win. And the gods decide their weapon will be a song. Not a spear, not a trick. The udgitha, the high chant of the Sama Veda. With this, they say, we'll overcome them. But a chant needs something to carry it. So the gods go looking for the right carrier, one part of a person after another, and the demons follow them to each one. Today: which breath can hold the song.
screen: `THE GODS AND THE DEMONS AT WAR.` → `THE GODS REACH FOR A SONG.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY IT?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, here's how it goes. First the gods sing the chant as the breath in the nose. The demons pierce it with evil. And that, the text says, is why we smell both the sweet and the foul. Next they try speech. Pierced again: that's why we speak both truth and falsehood. Then the eye, and we see both what's fitting and what isn't. Then the ear, and we hear both. Then the mind, and we think both kinds of thoughts. Try after try, each one cracks, because each one goes both ways. Then the gods sing the chant as the breath in the mouth, the main breath, the one that keeps a body alive. The demons rush at it, and they scatter, the text says, the way a lump of earth flung at a solid rock breaks into pieces. Notice what this story is doing. It's an explanation of everyday life, almost funny in its plainness: here's why your nose finds bad smells and your tongue tells lies. Every sense in us is mixed. But underneath them is a breath that simply keeps going, in and out, on good days and bad, choosing nothing. That breath is prana. And the Chandogya says that is what the high chant is sung as. The singer's song rides on the same breath that keeps the singer alive. So in this reading, the Sama Veda isn't sung from the senses or even from the mind first. It's sung from the breath.
screen: `NOSE, SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: PIERCED.` · `EACH ONE GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `THE MAIN BREATH: THE DEMONS SCATTER.` · `THE SONG RIDES ON PRANA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go down the gods' list, then rest where they did. Sit comfortably. Notice a smell in the room, any smell. Notice a sound. Notice what your eyes rest on. Notice a thought passing. Each one has its own mood, and that's fine. Then let all of them go, and find the breath moving through the mouth and throat. Not controlling it. Just letting it come and go, the plain breath underneath. When a sense pulls you away, come back to that breath. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there. The bell holds the time.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the high chant can't be carried by the senses or the mind. It's sung as the main breath, prana. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Today, when a sense or a thought pulls you two ways, come back for one breath to the breath that doesn't. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 1276 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG.`

howItsDone: The story of the gods, the demons and the breath is taught from the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, where the high chant is meditated on as the main breath, prana.

match.prompt: the gods' tries — tap the pairs.
pairs: the demons scatter like earth on rock

myth: in the story the gods fight the demons with spears
they reach for a song: the udgitha, the high chant.
speech fails because it can tell both truth and falsehood
the demons pierce it, and so speech goes both ways.
the demons break against the main breath like a lump of earth on rock
that's the Chandogya's picture: they scatter.

fork.setup: you're one of the gods. nose, speech, eye, ear and mind have all been pierced. what do you sing the chant as now?
options: the main breath, the breath in the mouth
fork.reveal: the main breath. the demons rush at it and scatter like a lump of earth flung at a rock. the song rides on the breath that keeps you alive.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, life-breath. In Chandogya 1.2 the high chant is sung as the main breath.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant is sung with the voice, and that's that.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the high chant is sung as the main breath, the one the demons can't pierce.
what a scholar hears: mukhya prāṇa, the 'chief breath' in the mouth, set against the senses, each of which works both ways (Chandogya 1.2.1–7).

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.2.1–8 (the gods and demons; the udgitha as nose-breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, then the main breath)

notes: Paraphrase of Chandogya 1.2.1–8: confirm the order of the five pierced faculties (nose-breath, speech, eye, ear, mind) and the image of the clod of earth striking a rock.
'Both sides are children of the same creator' renders the text's devāsurā ... prājāpatyāḥ; confirm.
'The breath in the mouth, the main breath' renders mukhya prāṇa / āsanya prāṇa; confirm wording.
'Almost funny in its plainness' is tone, not a claim about the text; cut if a Keeper finds it light.
The line 'demons' is used for asuras; some teachers prefer 'asuras' or 'anti-gods'.
Editor pass: replaced the narrator's count 'five tries' with 'try after try' (claims rule); story order checked against Chandogya 1.2 and left as written.
